summary: Marks the fiftieth anniversary of the RFC Series. It includes reflections from people involved at key points, a review of where the Series stands, and thoughts on its next fifty years. It updates the perspectives in RFC 2555 and RFC 5540.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a birthday card for the RFC series after fifty years, full of stories from people who helped and ideas for the future.

questions: when was the first rfc published
subtitle: The RFC Series turns fifty: personal histories of how it began and was run, and questions about its next fifty years.

tldr.problem: The RFC Series reached its fiftieth anniversary in 2019, and its history and future needed to be recorded from the people who shaped it.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out a table of key moments from 1969 to 2017, five first-person perspectives (Crocker, Cerf, Daigle, Brownlee, Ginoza), and the editor's views on preservation, the RFC format and the stream structure.
tldr.outcome: It updates the perspectives of RFC 2555 and RFC 5540 and is a historical record. It sets no standard and asks for no protocol changes.

today: RFC 8700 is an Informational document of December 2019 from the IAB, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 2555 and RFC 5540, the earlier anniversary retrospectives.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The RFC Series began in April 1969 with the publication of Host Software by Steve Crocker. Early RFCs really were requests for comments, meant to start conversations rather than to be an archival record. Today, the text says, over 8500 RFCs have been published, accepted through the IETF, the IAB, the IRTF and the Independent Submissions streams.

The goal of the Series is to be a canonical source for the material the RFC Editor publishes and to preserve it in perpetuity. The RFC Editor role was formalized by RFC 902 in July 1984, and Jon Postel, the first RFC Editor, defined it by his actions. The document warns that personal narratives give only one lens on events, and it updates RFC 2555 and RFC 5540.
sections.plainLanguage: A very old club writes down its story after fifty years. It says up front that each person remembers things a little differently.

sections.title: Key Moments in RFC History
sections.content:
Table 1 of the RFC lists dated markers. Some of them are listed here.

  • April 1969: the first RFC. April 1971: the first distribution of RFCs over the network.
  • December 1972: the first mention of the Czar of Socket Numbers and the proposal for a formal registry.
  • April 1977: the first April 1st RFC.
  • January 1986: the first IETF meeting.
  • October 1989: the three-stage standards process first defined. October 2011: the two-stage process formalized.
  • March 1990, March 1992 and August 1995: the FYI, STD and BCP sub-series started. The FYI sub-series ended in August 2011.
  • 15 October 1998: Jon Postel's death.
  • July 2007: the administrative structure documented in RFC 4844, and the Independent Submission stream formalized.
  • August 2009: the RFC Editor organization established with a Series Editor, Independent Submission Editor, Production Center and Publisher.
  • May 2013: the RFC format change project started. April 2017: RFCs no longer printed to paper on publication.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a timeline on the wall, with a sticker for each big thing that happened, from the very first note to the last time anyone printed them on paper.

sections.title: How the Series Began and Grew
sections.content:
Steve Crocker recalls that the ARPANET procurement began in the summer of 1968, with four sites receiving Interface Message Processors. A small group of graduate students and staff called themselves the Network Working Group. In 1969 they decided to write down their discussions. The ground rules were that anyone could say anything and that nothing was official, so the notes were labeled Request for Comments. RFC 3 set the bar low: the minimum length for a note was one sentence.

Vint Cerf describes how Jon Postel took over as RFC manager in 1971 and recruited Joyce K. Reynolds and then Bob Braden. Leslie Daigle recounts how, in the mid 2000s, the RFC Editor function needed a new governance and funding model. This led to RFC 4844, which set out the Series mission and the roles of the parties, with IAB oversight.

Nevil Brownlee, Independent Submissions Editor from February 2010 through February 2018, describes the Independent Stream and the April 1st RFCs, which have no formal review and are checked by the ISE and the RSE. He reports 159 RFCs published in the Independent Stream during his eight years. Sandy Ginoza describes the RFC Editor growing from four people into the model set by RFC 5620 and refined by RFC 6635, with the Production Center and Publisher moving to Association Management Solutions in 2010.

Table 2 gives average yearly publication counts, from 80 in 1969 to 1972 and 20 in 1978 to 1982 up to 333 in 2008 to 2012. The all-time high of 385 was reached in 2011.
sections.plainLanguage: A few students began leaving friendly notes for each other, and the notes piled up. Over the years, more helpers joined and the club made proper rules so the notes kept coming.

sections.title: The Next Fifty Years
sections.content:
The editor argues that the Series started with communication over formality, and that while informality gave way to structure, the openness and a stable foundation must continue. Three topics follow.

  • Preservation. A proper digital archive is more than backed-up disks. RFC 8153 reviews what a digital archive means today. The Series will need new partners that can archive RFCs publicly and a format that stays archivable.
  • Format. US-ASCII has been the canonical format for decades but cannot meet many users' needs. The effort to change it started in 2012 and is described in RFC 7990. Sandy Ginoza expects multiple formats (XML, HTML, PDF/A-3 and TXT) allowing non-ASCII characters and SVG art.
  • Streams. The Series predates the IETF by eighteen years, but many see the two as the same thing. The question of whether to treat the distinction as artificial is left to the community, and conversations were underway.
sections.plainLanguage: The grown-ups ask how to keep the old stories safe, whether to switch from plain paper to fancier books, and whether the club and the library are really the same thing. Nobody has decided yet.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document says it has no security considerations and no IANA actions. It is a historical and reflective document and defines no protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a story book, not a machine, so there is nothing in it to break or to lock up.
